title: How long should a training video be?
summary: Make one training video per task, usually 1 to 3 minutes. What 26,610 videos made in Clueso and the edX research show, with lengths by training type.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- Make one training video per task and let that task set the length. Most software tasks take 1 to 3 minutes to show.
- Across 26,610 videos our customers exported from Clueso over the past year, the median ran 91 seconds and 89.4% finished inside 5 minutes.
- The best-known engagement study (Guo, Kim, and Rubin, 2014, 6.9 million edX sessions) found median watch time topped out at about 6 minutes, so treat 6 minutes as the upper limit for a single video.
- Anything bigger than one task becomes a series of short videos, with a written step-by-step guide for people who'd rather skim.


Say someone records the full walkthrough of a new expense tool, from login to the month-end export, and ships it as a 25-minute video. The employee who only needs to attach a receipt now scrubs through the whole thing looking for the 40 seconds that apply to them, and probably gives up before finding them.


What you really should be doing is make one video per task and let the task set the length. Most tasks take 1 to 3 minutes to show. Across the 26,610 videos our customers exported from Clueso over the past year, the median ran 91 seconds.


## How long should a training video be?


A training video should be as long as a task takes from start to finish at a normal speaking pace. For a single software workflow, that usually means 1 to 3 minutes. A policy explainer or an onboarding welcome rarely needs more than 5.


We looked at 26,610 videos our customers exported from Clueso between October 22, 2025, and October 21, 2026. You can read more about that data on[how long a software demo video should be](https://www.clueso.io/blog/what-makes-a-software-demo-video-work) .

The set covers every kind of business video made in Clueso, not only training, and it shows what teams ship rather than how long viewers kept watching. What it does show is how rarely teams go past 5 minutes: about one video in 10. Our guide to[making tutorial videos](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-make-tutorial-videos) uses the same figures.


## What does research say about training video length and engagement?


The "keep it under 6 minutes" advice you hear in training circles comes from a 2014 study. Philip Guo, Juho Kim, and Rob Rubin analyzed 6.9 million video-watching sessions across four edX courses and published the results as[How video production affects student engagement](https://pg.ucsd.edu/publications/edX-MOOC-video-production-and-engagement_LAS-2014.pdf) . Video length was the strongest predictor of engagement they found. Median watch time never went above about 6 minutes, however long the video ran, and students often stopped before the halfway point of videos longer than 9 minutes.


Two other findings matter more for workplace training. The shortest videos, 0 to 3 minutes, held attention best: in 75% of those sessions, students watched more than three quarters of the video. Students watched only 2 to 3 minutes of a how-to video regardless of its length, came back to tutorials more often than to lectures, and the authors concluded that people jump to the part they need.


## How long should each type of training video be?


Length changes with the job the video does. A software task video gets replayed at the moment someone is stuck, while a policy module gets watched once, start to finish, because someone has to sign off on it.

The compliance row is the one teams stretch most often. A course can run 40 minutes in total if the policy needs that much, but no single video should. Our roundup of[AI video tools for compliance training](https://www.clueso.io/blog/best-ai-video-tools-for-compliance-training) covers the tooling side.


## How do you tell if a training video is too long?


Running time on its own doesn't tell you much. A 4-minute video that walks through eight required fields can be the right length, while a 90-second one that spends 30 seconds on a loading screen is too long. These checks catch most of the problems:


1. **Count the questions it answers.** Write down the question a viewer has when they open the video, such as "how do I attach a receipt?" If you end up with two questions, you have two videos.
2. **Look for stretches where nothing new appears on screen.** Loading screens and restarted sentences add length without teaching anything. Cut those before you cut a step.
3. **Time the script.** At 130 words per minute, a 400-word script runs about 3 minutes. A script past 650 words is usually covering more than one task.
4. **Check where viewers drop off.** If your video host shows a retention graph, a steep drop in the first 15 seconds points at a slow opening.


## How do you break a long training video into chapters?


Split a long recording where one outcome ends and the next begins. List every task it covers, then give each task its own video with a title that names the task, like "Attach a receipt to an expense claim" instead of "Expenses part 3". Put a short overview first that says which video covers what.


If your player or LMS supports chapter markers, you can keep one file and mark each task instead. Separate videos usually cost less to maintain, though. When a button gets renamed, you fix one 90-second video instead of re-exporting a 20-minute one, and our guide to[updating a training video without re-recording it](https://www.clueso.io/blog/update-training-video-without-re-recording) covers how.


Pair the series with a written step-by-step guide, so people who come back for one step can find it without scrubbing through a video.


> Clueso does the splitting for you:[Clueso Cuts](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-cuts) breaks a long recording into short, topic-based clips on the Enterprise plan, and every video comes with a[step-by-step written guide](https://www.clueso.io/features/help-articles) built from the same recording.


Before you make anything new, open the longest training video in your library and write down every question it answers. The number on that list is how many videos it should be.


## Frequently asked questions


### How long should an employee training video be to keep people watching?


Keep each video to one task, which usually means 1 to 3 minutes, and keep any single video under 6 minutes. In a 2014 study of 6.9 million edX sessions, median watch time topped out at about 6 minutes. Among 26,610 videos our customers exported from Clueso over the past year, the median ran 91 seconds.


### Is the 6-minute rule for training videos real?


The number comes from real data, and the data has limits. The 2014 edX study found median engagement time was at most about 6 minutes regardless of video length, and the researchers recommended splitting lessons into chunks under 6 minutes. Its learners were students in math and science MOOCs, so treat 6 minutes as an upper limit for one video.


### How long should a compliance training video be?


Split compliance training into modules of one rule or scenario each, and keep each module under 6 minutes. The full course can run as long as the policy requires. If your LMS needs to track completion and scores, Clueso's[SCORM export](https://www.clueso.io/features/scorm-export) packages videos with quizzes as SCORM 1.2, SCORM 2004, or xAPI on the Enterprise plan.


### How many words of script fit in a 2-minute training video?


About 260 words, at the 130 words per minute that Columbia's Center for Teaching and Learning recommends for reading a script aloud. If you'd rather not narrate yourself, Clueso writes the script from your recording and reads it with[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) .


### Should you make one long training video or several short ones?


Several short ones, in most cases. Short videos are quicker to find, and a product change touches one of them instead of a long recording. If you already have long recordings, Clueso's[filler word removal](https://www.clueso.io/features/screen-recorder) trims pauses and restarts on every plan, and[Clueso Cuts](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-cuts) splits a long recording into separate clips on the Enterprise plan.
